How a tool's full description is shown

Dean asked for a redesign of how you read a tool's full description, in the MCP popover and in Settings › Integrations, and whether there are other annotations Luke could use. Every frame on this page is the real renderer (AgentServersButton, IntegrationsSection, MarkdownMessage, HoverCard) on main's compiled stylesheet, with synthetic tools shaped after PostHog's, Linear's, Neon's, Sentry's and Notion's public lists. Every frame is live: click into one, then use the arrows, Enter and Esc. Rendered in Chrome on Linux, so the system fonts are not the Mac's.

My pick: B, a detail page. In the popover, Enter (or a click) on a tool opens a page of its own in the popover's place, the way a server's page already opens. It has a back arrow, the tool's title with its raw name in mono, the server's hints, the description rendered as markdown, and a parameters list. Esc or ← goes back to the list with the filter and highlight kept. In Settings the same detail stands beside the list, and the arrows move through the tools with the detail following, so you can read all 155 of PostHog's tools without opening and closing each one. Both are one component, IntegrationToolDetail, under one list, IntegrationToolList.

Why B: only B gives a long, markdown-heavy description and a tool with 20+ parameters the room they need in a 340px popover. Today's inline expand (C) puts a scroller inside a scroller there, and a hover card (A) can't scroll or take the keyboard. The rows also get quieter: one line each, with the badge and nothing else.

Today

A row is the tool's name in mono, its badge, and two lines of the description. A press opens the row in place onto the whole description as plain, pre-wrapped text, so markdown shows its marks (## When to use, backticks, a table's pipes). The parameters are not shown anywhere, and on the popover's server page the arrows only scroll, so a tool can't be opened from the keyboard.

A · One-line rows, and a hover card

Each row is one line: the title, the raw name in mono, the badge, and the first sentence of the description. Resting the pointer on a row, or moving the highlight to it with the arrows, hangs a card beside the list (HoverCard/CardHead/CardRule, as a plan's or an agent tab's card hangs). The card shows the description rendered, the hints, and the parameters' names and types.

  • The list doesn't change shape, and scanning with the pointer is the fastest of the three.
  • Uses the card the window already hangs everywhere.
  • A card can't scroll, so a long description or a long parameter list is cut. A hover card is "a description the keyboard never enters" (tooltip.tsx), so you can't select, copy, or scroll it.
  • In the popover the card needs room past the popover's edge, which a narrow window or a right-hand agent pane doesn't have.

B · A detail page pick

The rows are one line, as in A, with a chevron on the highlighted row. In the popover, Enter, → or a click opens the tool's page in the popover's place. Its head is the same height as the server page's head: back, the title, and the raw name in mono. Below it are the hints (the badge first, then what else the server said), the description rendered by MarkdownMessage (paragraphs, lists, code, tables), and the parameters. Required parameters come first, each with its type, a description, and enum values as chips with the default outlined. On the page, ↑↓ scroll, and Esc, ← or Backspace go back. In Settings the page stands beside the list (a split pane); the arrows move the selection and the detail follows; Enter or → moves focus into the detail to scroll it; Esc or ← moves it back.

  • Unbounded room for the description and the parameters, scrolled as one page, with text you can select and copy.
  • Uses the popover's existing model: a server already opens as a page, and a tool is one level further down, with the same back, the same head, and Esc going up one level.
  • The Settings split makes reading a long list of tools a matter of the arrow keys.
  • One more level in the popover. Comparing two tools means going back and forth (in the popover; Settings shows them side by side).
  • If the Settings window is narrow, the split falls back to the popover's stacked page, so a narrow Settings page behaves like the popover.

C · An inline expand that renders

Today's model, done properly. A press or Enter opens the row in place onto the hints, the description rendered as markdown, and the parameters, held to 300px with its own scroll. One tool is open at a time.

  • The smallest change from today, and the neighboring tools stay in view.
  • In the popover, a long description is a scroller inside the list's scroller, about 300px tall, under a head that has scrolled away.
  • The wheel and the arrows have to decide which scroller they move.

Annotations: what each hint says, and where

Luke's wire already carries all four of the MCP spec's ToolAnnotations hints. The rows keep the two badges they wear today. The others show on the detail page only, so the rows stay quiet. A hint is shown only where the server sent it, never guessed from a name, and never read as its spec default when absent. Following the spec, destructiveHint and idempotentHint are read only on a tool that isn't read-only. The spec calls annotations hints that "clients MUST consider untrusted", so the page shows them as what the server says (the list's accessible name is "What PostHog's server says of this tool") and nothing acts on them.

The server sentRowDetailNeeds
readOnlyHint: trueRead-onlyRead-onlyUI only (today)
destructiveHint: true, not read-onlyDestructiveDestructiveUI only (today)
readOnlyHint: false and destructiveHint: false—Only adds, never deletesUI only
idempotentHint: true, not read-only—Safe to retryUI only
openWorldHint: true—Reaches outside PostHogUI only
openWorldHint: false—Only PostHog's own dataUI only
no hint, or no annotations—nothing—
title, or annotations.titleThe title, raw name in mono beside itTitle in the head, raw name beside itSmall wire change
iconsNot drawn in this round (see below)Wire change, and the service fetching the icon

What each part needs

PartNeedsHow
Detail page, rendered markdown, one-line rows, keyboardUI onlyOne shared IntegrationToolList plus IntegrationToolDetail, used by agent-servers.tsx and integrations-page.tsx.
Safe to retry, reaches outside / only its own data, only addsUI onlyAlready on the wire (integrationToolAnnotationsSchema).
Title as the display nameSmall wire changeintegration-wire.ts doesn't carry title today. mcp-tools.ts would read Tool.title, then annotations.title, the spec's order ("title, annotations.title, then name"; VS Code reads them the other way round). It keeps one bounded title, an optional key on the tools answer and on IntegrationTool. The search also finds a tool by its title.
ParametersWire changeThe service reads inputSchema's top-level properties and required into a bounded list: name, a short type (string, string[], string | null, enum, object), required, description, enum values and default. Nested schemas are named by their type, not expanded. Capped at about 64 parameters and 300 characters each. The model never reads this list; it is only for a person picking servers, like the rest of the answer.
A long description read wholeOne-line server changemcp-tools.ts keeps 2,000 characters of a description (DESCRIPTION_MAX_CHARS). The detail page is the first place a long description is read whole, so raise it to about 8,000.
Tool iconsWire change and a service fetch; suggest deferringThe spec added icons in 2025-11-25: https or data: URIs. The panel's CSP admits img-src 'self' data: and GitHub's and Google's avatar hosts only. A URL loaded from the renderer would also tell the provider when the developer opened the list. So the service would fetch each icon, bound its size, and hand it on as data:. Until a provider we connect sends tool icons (not checked: it needs the live servers), the server's own mark in the page head says whose tool it is.

What this suggests: no one has solved this well, and the closest are VS Code's one-line description in the picker plus a markdown description where it matters. Nobody shows a parameter table outside a call, and a Cursor user missed exactly that. The MCP blog says no client yet surfaces annotations beyond read-only or destructive (blog). The spec (2026-07-28) names the display-name order and asks clients to treat annotations from an untrusted server as untrusted.
